questions.q: What does a Basic Authentication request actually put in the Authorization header?
options: The username and password joined with a colon and base64-encoded, sent on every request
A one-time access token issued by an OAuth authorization server
A client certificate that proves the caller's identity
An irreversible hash of the password
questions.explain: Basic Auth literally base64-encodes username:password and resends that same encoded string on every call — there's no token or certificate involved.

questions.q: Why doesn't base64 encoding protect a Basic Auth credential from someone who intercepts the request?
options: Base64 only works for numeric passwords
ServiceNow disables base64 decoding for security reasons
Base64 is a reversible encoding scheme, not a cipher — decoding it back to the original username:password takes no key at all
Base64-encoded text is always shorter than the original, which hides its structure
questions.explain: Base64 just re-represents bytes as text; reversing it needs no secret, so HTTPS — not the encoding — is what actually protects the credential in transit.

questions.q: Which of these is a real structural weakness of Basic Auth compared to OAuth 2.0, even when used correctly over HTTPS?
options: Basic Auth cannot be attached to a REST Message's Authentication Profile
The real username and password are sent on every single request, instead of a short-lived token obtained once and reused
Basic Auth requires a MID Server for every call
Basic Auth only works with SOAP, not REST
questions.explain: OAuth exchanges a token once and reuses or refreshes it; Basic Auth re-sends the actual credential on every call for as long as the integration runs.

questions.q: Why is revoking access for one integration that uses Basic Auth often harder than it sounds?
options: ServiceNow doesn't allow Authentication Profiles to be deleted
Basic Auth credentials cannot be changed once they're set
Revoking access always requires contacting the external vendor directly

If multiple integrations share the same service account's password, changing it to cut off one integration breaks all of them, requiring the new password to be redistributed to the ones that should keep working
questions.explain: Because Basic Auth has no per-integration token, revocation really means "change a shared password" — blunt when several integrations depend on that one credential.

questions.q: Given its real weaknesses, when does this lesson say Basic Auth is still a reasonable choice?
options: For every production integration with an external financial system
Only when the external API requires mutual TLS
For a quick internal test, a sandbox instance, or a legacy API that genuinely offers no stronger option — with a plan to replace it before going live with a partner that supports OAuth
Never — Basic Auth should not be used under any circumstance
questions.explain: Basic Auth isn't banned outright — it's a legitimate fast path for low-stakes or no-alternative cases, just not the production default.
